\section{Introduction}

Approximation theory for neural networks has two halves. The \emph{upper-bound}
half exhibits architectures reaching a prescribed accuracy and counts their
resources; the \emph{lower-bound} half proves a competing architecture cannot do
the same with fewer. A separation theorem is a matched pair.

For piecewise-linear activations the lower-bound half has a canonical
mechanism: a one-hidden-layer ReLU network is a polyline with at most as many
kinks as it has units, and polylines are poor at curvature. For \emph{analytic}
activations no such mechanism exists, and one expects---but must prove---that
the extra smoothness buys something.

The EML activation $x \mapsto e^{ax+b}-\log(cx+d)$ is analytic on its domain
and combines two very different behaviours in one unit: an exponential branch
with unbounded growth and all derivatives positive, and a slowly varying concave
logarithmic branch. This paper answers: what exactly does that smoothness buy,
and what does it cost?

Section~\ref{sec:model} fixes the model. Section~\ref{sec:square} constructs the
width-two squaring layer and proves the two-sided rate $\Theta(h^{2})$ together
with the gradient estimate, and shows a naive forward-difference construction is
genuinely only first order. Section~\ref{sec:depth} proves depth composes.
Section~\ref{sec:relu} proves the shallow ReLU lower bounds from scratch.
Section~\ref{sec:sep} assembles the separation. Section~\ref{sec:pol} develops
the multiplication gate, quadratic forms, and the transfer of the barrier to two
inputs. Section~\ref{sec:softplus} proves the converse containment.
Sections~\ref{sec:alg}--\ref{sec:disc} give algorithms, numerics and discussion.

A one-sentence summary, kept in view throughout: \emph{width, depth and weight
magnitude are three currencies, and an analytic activation can pay in any of
them, whereas a piecewise-linear one can pay only in width.}

\section{The model}\label{sec:model}

\begin{definition}[EML neuron]
An \emph{EML neuron} is determined by four real parameters and computes
$\mathcal N_{a,b,c,d}(x)=e^{ax+b}-\log(cx+d)$, defined where $cx+d>0$. Taking
$c=0$, $d=1$ switches the logarithmic branch off, since $\log 1 = 0$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[EML layer]
An \emph{EML layer of width $k$} consists of neurons $\mathcal N_1,\dots,\mathcal
N_k$, read-out weights $\gamma_i\in\R$ and a bias $\beta\in\R$, and computes
$L(x)=\beta+\sum_{i=1}^{k}\gamma_i\mathcal N_i(x)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Depth]
A \emph{depth-two EML network} is a composition $L_2\circ L_1$ of two layers, or
more generally a family of parallel chains with an affine read-out and an affine
skip connection,
\[
  \mathcal D(x)=s_0+s_1x+\sum_{i=1}^{k}\gamma_i\,
    \mathcal N^{(2)}_i\!\left(\mathcal N^{(1)}_i(x)\right).
\]
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Shallow ReLU network]\label{def:relunet}
With $\relu(t)=\max(t,0)$, a \emph{one-hidden-layer ReLU network with $k$ units}
is
\[
  R_k(x)=c_0+c_1x+\sum_{i=1}^{k}a_i\,\relu(w_ix+b_i),
\]
with arbitrary real parameters. The affine skip connection is granted for free,
so all lower bounds below hold a fortiori without it.
\end{definition}

\section{A width-two EML layer squares to second order}\label{sec:square}

\begin{definition}[Central-difference squaring layer]
For $h\neq0$ let $S_h$ be the EML layer of width two with neurons
$(h,0,0,1)$ and $(-h,0,0,1)$, read-out weights $1/h^{2}$ each, and bias
$-2/h^{2}$.
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}\label{prop:sform}
For $h\neq0$, $\displaystyle S_h(x)=\frac{e^{hx}+e^{-hx}-2}{h^{2}}
=\frac{2(\cosh(hx)-1)}{h^{2}}$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Both logarithmic branches read $\log(0\cdot x+1)=0$; substitute and simplify.
\end{proof}

Thus $S_h$ is the second central difference of the exponential, with Maclaurin
series $S_h(x)=x^{2}+\tfrac{1}{12}h^{2}x^{4}+\tfrac{1}{360}h^{4}x^{6}+\cdots$,
and $S_h(0)=0$.

\begin{lemma}[Quartic Taylor bound for $2\cosh$]\label{lem:cosh}
For $|u|\le1$, $\bigl|e^{u}+e^{-u}-2-u^{2}\bigr|\le u^{4}/6$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Apply the fifth-order Taylor estimate to $e^{u}$ and to $e^{-u}$ (admissible as
$|{\pm}u|\le1$). All odd powers cancel in the sum; the constant and quadratic
terms are subtracted; the surviving quartic term is $2u^{4}/4!=u^{4}/12$, and
the fifth-order remainders contribute at most an explicit constant times
$|u|^{5}\le u^{4}$. Collecting gives $u^{4}/6$. The sharp asymptotic constant is
$1/12$; the factor two is the price of a remainder bound valid uniformly on
$|u|\le1$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Second-order squaring]\label{thm:sq}
For $h\neq0$ and $|hx|\le1$,
\[
  \bigl|S_h(x)-x^{2}\bigr|\;\le\;\frac{h^{2}x^{4}}{6}.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
By Proposition~\ref{prop:sform},
$S_h(x)-x^{2}=\bigl(e^{hx}+e^{-hx}-2-(hx)^{2}\bigr)/h^{2}$;
Lemma~\ref{lem:cosh} with $u=hx$ bounds the numerator by $h^{4}x^{4}/6$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}\label{cor:rate}
For $0<h\le1$ and $x\in[0,1]$ we have $|S_h(x)-x^{2}|\le h^{2}/6$; with $h=1/n$,
$\max_{[0,1]}|S_{1/n}(x)-x^{2}|\le 1/(6n^{2})$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{corollary}[Constant width suffices]\label{cor:width2}
For every $\varepsilon>0$, taking $h=\min(1,\varepsilon)$, the \emph{width-two}
layer $S_h$ satisfies $|S_h(x)-x^{2}|\le\varepsilon$ on $[0,1]$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{lemma}[Lower Taylor estimate]\label{lem:coshlow}
For $0<h\le1$, $\;e^{h}+e^{-h}\ge 2+h^{2}+h^{4}/14$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
A partial sum of the exponential series underestimates $e^{h}$ for $h\ge0$;
retain terms through $h^{4}$. For $e^{-h}$ use a two-sided fifth-order remainder
estimate and absorb the resulting $h^{5},h^{6}$ terms into $h^{4}$ using
$h\le1$. The surviving quartic coefficient is still at least $1/14$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Sharpness]\label{thm:sqlow}
For $0<h\le1$, $\;|S_h(1)-1|\ge h^{2}/14$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
$S_h(1)-1=(e^{h}+e^{-h}-2-h^{2})/h^{2}\ge (h^{4}/14)/h^{2}$ by
Lemma~\ref{lem:coshlow}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Two-sided rate]
For $0<h\le1$ the uniform error of $S_h$ on $[0,1]$ lies between $h^{2}/14$ and
$h^{2}/6$; it is $\Theta(h^{2})$ and the exponent is exact.
\end{theorem}

\subsection*{The naive construction is genuinely slower}

The forward difference $F_h(x)=\tfrac{2}{h^{2}}(e^{hx}-1-hx)
= x^{2}+\tfrac{1}{3}hx^{3}+\cdots$ uses a single exponential neuron.

\begin{theorem}[First-order barrier]\label{thm:fwd}
For every $h>0$, $\;\tfrac{2}{h^{2}}(e^{h}-1-h)-1\ \ge\ h/3$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
$1+h+h^{2}/2+h^{3}/6\le e^{h}$ for $h\ge0$; subtract and multiply by $2/h^{2}$
to obtain $h/3$ plus a nonnegative remainder.
\end{proof}

Numerically the ratio tends to $1/3$ from above, so the constant is sharp: the
improvement from $\Theta(h)$ to $\Theta(h^{2})$ is real.

\subsection*{Gradients}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:sinh}
For $|u|\le1$, $\;|e^{u}-e^{-u}-2u|\le |u|^{3}/2$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{theorem}[Second-order gradients at width two]\label{thm:grad}
For $0<h\le1$ and $x\in[0,1]$,
\[
  \left|\frac{e^{hx}-e^{-hx}}{h}-2x\right|\;\le\;\frac{h^{2}}{2}.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The left-hand quantity is $S_h'(x)-(x^{2})'$; write it as
$(e^{hx}-e^{-hx}-2hx)/h$ and apply Lemma~\ref{lem:sinh} with $u=hx$, using
$|hx|^{3}\le h^{3}$.
\end{proof}

\section{Depth composes: the quartic}\label{sec:depth}

\begin{theorem}[Depth-two quartic]\label{thm:quartic}
For $0<h\le 1/2$ and $x\in[0,1]$, $\;|S_h(S_h(x))-x^{4}|\le h^{2}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Put $y=S_h(x)$ and split
$S_h(S_h(x))-x^{4}=\bigl(S_h(y)-y^{2}\bigr)+\bigl(y^{2}-x^{4}\bigr)$.

\emph{Stability.} By Corollary~\ref{cor:rate}, $|y-x^{2}|\le h^{2}/6\le 1/24$ and
$0\le x^{2}\le1$, so $|y|\le 25/24$ and hence $|hy|\le\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac{25}{24}<1$:
exactly the hypothesis needed to apply Theorem~\ref{thm:sq} at $y$. This is the
sole use of $h\le1/2$, and it is the mechanism by which depth composes safely.

\emph{First term.} Theorem~\ref{thm:sq} at $y$ gives
$|S_h(y)-y^{2}|\le h^{2}y^{4}/6\le h^{2}/3$, since $y^{4}\le (25/24)^{4}\le2$.

\emph{Second term.} $y^{2}-x^{4}=(y-x^{2})(y+x^{2})$ and $|y+x^{2}|\le 25/24+1$,
so $|y^{2}-x^{4}|\le \tfrac{h^{2}}{6}\cdot\tfrac{49}{24}\le h^{2}/2$.

Adding, $h^{2}/3+h^{2}/2\le h^{2}$.
\end{proof}

\section{The shallow ReLU barrier}\label{sec:relu}

\begin{lemma}[Breakpoint-free interval]\label{lem:pigeon}
Let $w,b\in\R^{k}$. Among the $k+1$ intervals
$I_j=\bigl(\tfrac{j}{k+1},\tfrac{j+1}{k+1}\bigr)$, $j=0,\dots,k$, at least one
contains no breakpoint: for all $x\in I_j$ and all $i$ with $w_i\neq0$ we have
$w_ix+b_i\neq0$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
A unit with $w_i\neq0$ has exactly one breakpoint $-b_i/w_i$; a unit with
$w_i=0$ is constant and has none. At most $k$ points in $k+1$ disjoint open
intervals leave one empty.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Affinity on the empty box]\label{lem:affine}
If $wx+b\neq0$ throughout an interval $I$, then $x\mapsto\relu(wx+b)$ agrees on
$I$ with a fixed affine function (either $wx+b$ or $0$, by continuity and the
intermediate value theorem). Consequently, under Lemma~\ref{lem:pigeon} there
are $\alpha,\beta$ with $R_k(x)=\alpha x+\beta$ for all $x\in I_j$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proposition}[Structural core]\label{prop:gap}
For every $k$ and every parameter choice there exist $0\le p<q\le1$ with
$q-p=1/(k+1)$ and $\alpha,\beta\in\R$ such that $R_k(x)=\alpha x+\beta$ on
$(p,q)$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{lemma}[A line cannot follow a parabola]\label{lem:secdiff}
Let $p<q$, $L=q-p$, and suppose $|x^{2}-(\alpha x+\beta)|\le\varepsilon$ for all
$x\in(p,q)$. Then $\varepsilon\ge L^{2}/32$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Evaluate at $x_1=p+L/4$, $x_2=p+L/2$, $x_3=p+3L/4$. The second difference
$g\mapsto g(x_1)-2g(x_2)+g(x_3)$ annihilates affine functions and maps $x^{2}$
to $2(L/4)^{2}=L^{2}/8$; hence $L^{2}/8\le 4\varepsilon$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Shallow ReLU cannot square]\label{thm:relulow}
For every $k\ge0$ and all parameters,
\[
  \max_{x\in[0,1]}\bigl|x^{2}-R_k(x)\bigr|\;\ge\;\frac{1}{32(k+1)^{2}}.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Combine Proposition~\ref{prop:gap} with Lemma~\ref{lem:secdiff} at
$L=1/(k+1)$.
\end{proof}

The case $k=0$ is included and reads $\varepsilon\ge1/32$. The optimal constant
for Lemma~\ref{lem:secdiff} is $1/8$ (endpoints); $1/32$ is the price of
sampling interior quarter points, which keeps the argument valid on an open
interval. Only the exponent matters below.

\begin{theorem}[Shallow ReLU cannot match the slope]\label{thm:relugrad}
For every $k$ and all parameters there is an interval $(p,q)\subseteq[0,1]$ of
length $1/(k+1)$ on which $R_k$ is affine with slope $\alpha$, and a point
$x\in(p,q)$ with $|\alpha-2x|\ge 1/(2(k+1))$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
On $(p,q)$ the true slope $2x$ sweeps an interval of length $2/(k+1)$ while the
network's slope is the constant $\alpha$; one of the quarter points
$p+L/4$, $p+3L/4$ realises a discrepancy at least $L/2=1/(2(k+1))$.
\end{proof}

\section{The separation theorem}\label{sec:sep}

\begin{theorem}[Width separation on $x^{2}$]\label{thm:sep}
For every $\varepsilon>0$:
\begin{enumerate}
\item there is $h>0$ such that the EML layer $S_h$, of width $2$, satisfies
$|S_h(x)-x^{2}|\le\varepsilon$ on $[0,1]$;
\item every one-hidden-layer ReLU network with $k$ units achieving the same
accuracy satisfies $(k+1)^{2}\ge 1/(32\varepsilon)$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(1) is Corollary~\ref{cor:width2}; (2) is Theorem~\ref{thm:relulow} rearranged.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Explicit exchange rate]
To match the accuracy $1/(6n^{2})$ of $S_{1/n}$, a shallow ReLU network needs
$3n^{2}\le 16(k+1)^{2}$, i.e.\ $k+1\ge \tfrac{\sqrt3}{4}n\approx0.433\,n$, while
the EML width stays at $2$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{remark}[What is being traded]
The read-out weights of $S_h$ are $\pm 1/h^{2}$ and the two exponentials nearly
cancel: at accuracy $\varepsilon=h^{2}/6$ the coefficients have magnitude
$\sim 1/(6\varepsilon)$. The separation is width against weight magnitude, and
should be stated as such; see Section~\ref{sec:disc}.
\end{remark}

\section{Polarisation: products, quadratic forms, two inputs}\label{sec:pol}

\begin{definition}[EML multiplication gate]
\[
  P_h(x,y)=\frac{S_h(x+y)-S_h(x-y)}{4}
  =\frac{e^{h(x+y)}+e^{-h(x+y)}-e^{h(x-y)}-e^{-h(x-y)}}{4h^{2}},
\]
a layer of width four, from the polarisation identity
$xy=\tfrac14\bigl((x+y)^{2}-(x-y)^{2}\bigr)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Accuracy of the gate]\label{thm:gate}
If $|h(x+y)|\le1$ and $|h(x-y)|\le1$ then
\[
  |P_h(x,y)-xy|\;\le\;\frac{h^{2}\bigl((x+y)^{4}+(x-y)^{4}\bigr)}{24}.
\]
In particular for $0<h\le1/2$ and $x,y\in[0,1]$, $|P_h(x,y)-xy|\le h^{2}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:sq} at $x\pm y$, combine by the triangle inequality and
divide by four. On $[0,1]^{2}$, $(x+y)^{4}\le16$ and $(x-y)^{4}\le1$, giving
$17h^{2}/24\le h^{2}$; the hypotheses hold because $h\le1/2$ and $|x\pm y|\le2$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Sharpness of the gate]\label{thm:gatelow}
For $0<h\le1/2$, $\;|P_h(1,1)-1|\ge 2h^{2}/7$; hence the gate's uniform error on
$[0,1]^{2}$ is $\Theta(h^{2})$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
$S_h(0)=0$, so $P_h(1,1)-1=\bigl(e^{2h}+e^{-2h}-2-(2h)^{2}\bigr)/(4h^{2})$;
Lemma~\ref{lem:coshlow} at $2h\in(0,1]$ bounds the numerator below by
$16h^{4}/14$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Every quadratic form is one EML layer]\label{thm:quad}
Let $A\in\R^{n\times n}$, $q(x)=\sum_{i,j}A_{ij}x_ix_j$ and $0<h\le1/2$. Then for
all $x\in[0,1]^{n}$,
\[
  \Bigl|\sum_{i,j}A_{ij}P_h(x_i,x_j)-q(x)\Bigr|
  \;\le\;h^{2}\sum_{i,j}|A_{ij}|,
\]
and the left-hand network is a single EML layer of width at most $4n^{2}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Subtract termwise and apply Theorem~\ref{thm:gate} to each product together with
the triangle inequality.
\end{proof}

The constant is \emph{dimension-free}: the dimension enters only through the
coefficient mass $\sum_{i,j}|A_{ij}|$.

\begin{definition}
A one-hidden-layer ReLU network in two inputs with $k$ units is
$R^{(2)}_k(x,y)=c_0+c_1x+c_2y+\sum_i a_i\relu(w_ix+v_iy+b_i)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Diagonal restriction]\label{lem:diag}
$R^{(2)}_k(x,x)$ is a univariate one-hidden-layer ReLU network with $k$ units,
with hidden weights $w_i+v_i$, biases $b_i$, read-out $a_i$ and skip connection
$c_0+(c_1+c_2)x$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{theorem}[Products are as hard as squares for shallow ReLU]\label{thm:prodlow}
If $|xy-R^{(2)}_k(x,y)|\le\varepsilon$ on $[0,1]^{2}$ then
$\varepsilon\ge 1/(32(k+1)^{2})$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Restrict to $y=x$: the target becomes $x^{2}$ and, by Lemma~\ref{lem:diag}, the
network becomes a univariate $k$-unit shallow ReLU network; apply
Theorem~\ref{thm:relulow}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Product separation]
For every $\varepsilon>0$ the width-four gate reaches accuracy $\varepsilon$ on
$[0,1]^{2}$ (take $h=\min(1/2,\varepsilon)$), whereas every bivariate shallow
ReLU network doing the same has $(k+1)^{2}\ge 1/(32\varepsilon)$.
\end{theorem}

\section{The converse: depth two contains shallow ReLU}\label{sec:softplus}

Let $\softplus(t)=\log(1+e^{t})$: an exponential neuron followed by a
logarithmic one, i.e.\ a depth-two EML chain.

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:sp}
For all $t$, $\;\relu(t)\le\softplus(t)\le\relu(t)+\log 2$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
For $t\le0$: $\relu(t)=0\le\log(1+e^{t})\le\log2$ since $e^{t}\le1$. For $t>0$:
$\log(1+e^{t})=t+\log(1+e^{-t})$ with $0<\log(1+e^{-t})\le\log2$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Scaled softplus approximates ReLU]\label{thm:sp}
For $M>0$ and all $t$, $\;\bigl|M^{-1}\log(1+e^{Mt})-\relu(t)\bigr|\le \log2/M$,
with equality at $t=0$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:sp} at $Mt$, use $\relu(Mt)=M\relu(t)$ and divide by $M$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Emulation]\label{thm:emul}
For $M>0$ there is an explicit depth-two EML network with $k$ parallel chains
---the $i$-th being $x\mapsto e^{M(w_ix+b_i)}$ followed by
$u\mapsto 1-\log(1+u)$, read out with weight $-a_i/M$, plus the skip connection
$c_0+c_1x$---whose uniform distance to $R_k$ on all of $\R$ is at most
$\bigl(\sum_i|a_i|\bigr)\log2/M$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Domination]\label{thm:dom}
If a $k$-unit shallow ReLU network approximates $f$ within $\varepsilon$ on a set
$S$, then for every $\delta>0$ there is a depth-two EML network with $k$ chains
approximating $f$ within $\varepsilon+\delta$ on $S$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Choose $M\ge\max\{1,(\sum_i|a_i|)\log2/\delta\}$ in Theorem~\ref{thm:emul} and
apply the triangle inequality.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}[Interpolant as a ReLU network]
For $f:[0,1]\to\R$ and $N\ge1$ let $\sigma_j=N(f(\tfrac{j+1}{N})-f(\tfrac{j}{N}))$
and $\lambda_j=\sigma_j-\sigma_{j-1}$ (with $\sigma_{-1}=0$). Then
$\Pi_Nf(x)=f(0)+\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}\lambda_j\relu\!\left(x-\tfrac{j}{N}\right)$
is a width-$N$ shallow ReLU network equal, on each piece, to the linear
interpolant of $f$ at the endpoints.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Interpolation error]\label{thm:interp}
If $f$ is $L$-Lipschitz on $[0,1]$ then
$\max_{[0,1]}|f-\Pi_Nf|\le 2L/N$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
On the $j$-th piece $\Pi_Nf(x)$ is a convex combination of $f(j/N)$ and
$f((j+1)/N)$, each within $L/N$ of $f(x)$ since the piece has length $1/N$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Jackson rate for depth-two EML]\label{thm:jackson}
Let $f$ be $L$-Lipschitz on $[0,1]$, $N\ge1$, $\delta>0$. There is a depth-two
EML network with $N$ chains whose uniform error on $[0,1]$ is at most
$2L/N+\delta$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Combine Theorems~\ref{thm:interp} and \ref{thm:dom}.
\end{proof}

\section{Algorithms and numerical corroboration}\label{sec:alg}

\begin{algorithmbox}[Central-difference squaring layer]
Given $\varepsilon$, set $h=\min(1,\sqrt{6\varepsilon})$ and return the width-two
layer with parameters $(h,0,0,1)$, $(-h,0,0,1)$, read-out $(1/h^{2},1/h^{2})$ and
bias $-2/h^{2}$. Evaluation costs two exponentials; guaranteed error
$h^{2}/6\le\varepsilon$ on $[0,1]$.
\end{algorithmbox}

\begin{algorithmbox}[Quadratic-form layer]
Given $A$ and $\varepsilon$, set $h=\min(1/2,\sqrt{\varepsilon/\|A\|_{1,1}})$ and
return $\sum_{i,j}A_{ij}P_h(x_i,x_j)$: width $\le4n^{2}$, cost $O(n^{2})$
transcendental evaluations, guaranteed error $h^{2}\|A\|_{1,1}\le\varepsilon$.
\end{algorithmbox}

\begin{algorithmbox}[Softplus emulator]
Given $(a,w,b,c_0,c_1)$ and slack $\delta$, set
$M=\max\{1,(\sum_i|a_i|)\log2/\delta\}$ and return the chains of
Theorem~\ref{thm:emul}; uniform emulation error $\le\delta$.
\end{algorithmbox}

\section{Discussion}\label{sec:disc}

\subsection*{What the trade-off actually is}

On the Lipschitz class the rate is $\Theta(1/N)$ for both models
(Theorem~\ref{thm:jackson}); a Lipschitz function carries no second-order
information to exploit. On smooth targets the correct statement is not about
width at all: Theorem~\ref{thm:sq} and Theorem~\ref{thm:sqlow} give
$\Theta(h^{2})$ at the \emph{fixed} width two, and Theorem~\ref{thm:relulow}
shows this is unattainable for shallow ReLU at any fixed width. The resource
actually spent is weight magnitude: read-out coefficients $1/h^{2}$ buy accuracy
$h^{2}$. The gradient results sharpen the contrast, $O(h^{2})$ at width two
against $\Omega(1/k)$ at width $k$; this is the more consequential half whenever
the derivative of the learned function is the object of interest.

\subsection*{Limitations}

\emph{Weight magnitude.} The EML upper bounds use coefficients of size
$\Theta(1/\varepsilon)$ and near-cancelling exponentials, placing a round-off
floor at roughly $\sqrt{u}$ in the achievable accuracy ($u$ the unit roundoff)
---the classical trade-off of central-difference differentiation.

\emph{Class of targets.} The width-two phenomenon is specific to targets whose
Taylor series the activation reproduces cheaply: squares, products, quadratic
forms, and (via depth) powers $x^{2^{m}}$.

\emph{Model of ReLU.} The lower bounds concern \emph{one} hidden layer; deep
ReLU networks achieve $O(4^{-d})$ on $x^{2}$ with $d$ layers by the sawtooth
construction. Section~\ref{sec:softplus} adds that depth-two EML also contains
shallow ReLU, so the comparison at small fixed depth is one-sided.

\subsection*{Future directions}

\textbf{C1. Bounded-weight separation.} Fix $W\ge1$ and cap all EML weights by
$W$ in absolute value. Conjecture: approximating $x^{2}$ to accuracy
$\varepsilon$ then requires width $k\ge c\,\varepsilon^{-1/2}/\log W$, and this
is attained; the constant-width phenomenon is thus exactly a statement about
weight magnitude, and under a polynomial weight budget the two models are
separated only by a logarithmic factor. The key insight is that the width-two
construction spends $1/h^{2}$ of read-out magnitude to buy $h^{2}$ of accuracy,
so magnitude and width are interchangeable currencies and the bound belongs in
the total budget $k\log W$. Both halves of the ledger are in place: the upper
bound exhibits the exchange rate, and the pigeonhole argument is a template for
a lower bound that counts \emph{pieces}, which under a weight budget an EML
layer also has.

\textbf{C2. Depth is worth an exponent for analytic targets.} Conjecture: for
every $m\ge1$ the composition $S_h^{\circ m}$ approximates $x^{2^{m}}$ on
$[0,1]$ with uniform error $\le C_mh^{2}$, $C_m\le 2^{m}$, while any depth-one
EML layer of width $k$ needs $k\ge c\,2^{m}/(1+|\log h|)$ for the same accuracy:
depth doubles the polynomial degree per layer at constant width.
Theorem~\ref{thm:quartic} is the case $m=2$ with $C_2=1$, and its proof used
only that the first layer's output stays in a fixed compact set---an invariant
that iterates.

\textbf{C3. Beyond quadratic forms.} Products give monomials by iteration and
monomials give polynomials; the natural target is a Bernstein- or
Chebyshev-type theorem identifying which polynomial classes admit EML networks
of width polynomial in the degree with dimension-free constants, and how the
coefficient mass generalises to a Barron-type norm.

\textbf{C4. Numerical stabilisation.} Since the obstruction to small $h$ is
cancellation, stably evaluated variants (via $\mathrm{expm1}$, or Richardson
extrapolation across two scales, which would give $\Theta(h^{4})$ at width four)
should be analysed under a fixed floating-point format.

\textbf{C5. Training dynamics.} All results here concern expressivity. Whether
gradient descent \emph{finds} the central-difference configuration---a delicate
near-cancellation of two large exponentials---is a separate and open question.

\section{Conclusion}

The parabola already separates two families of networks. A single EML layer of
two neurons reaches any accuracy on $x^{2}$, with error exactly $\Theta(h^{2})$
and a simultaneously $O(h^{2})$-accurate derivative, while every
one-hidden-layer ReLU network with $k$ units errs by at least $1/(32(k+1)^{2})$
and misestimates the slope by $\Omega(1/k)$. Polarisation extends this to
products and to all quadratic forms with a dimension-free constant, and the ReLU
barrier transfers to the bivariate product without loss. Conversely, softplus
embeds every shallow ReLU network into a depth-two EML network of equal width,
so the smooth model is never worse and inherits the optimal $\Theta(1/N)$
Lipschitz rate. The phrase ``depth--width trade-off'' is therefore incomplete:
for analytic activations a third currency, weight magnitude, enters, and the
honest question is what the exchange rates become when all three are budgeted at
once.

  4. The depth-2 composition S_h(S_h(x)) approximates x^4 with error <= h^2.

Self-contained: standard library only (math, random, itertools, typing).
Run with:  python3 demo.py
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import math
import random
from itertools import product
from typing import Callable, List, Sequence, Tuple

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. The EML model
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def eml_neuron(a: float, b: float, c: float, d: float, x: float) -> float:
    """A single EML neuron:  x -> exp(a x + b) - log(c x + d).

    Setting c = 0, d = 1 switches the logarithmic branch off (log 1 = 0).
    """
    return math.exp(a * x + b) - math.log(c * x + d)


def eml_layer(
    neurons: Sequence[Tuple[float, float, float, float]],
    out: Sequence[float],
    bias: float,
    x: float,
) -> float:
    """An EML layer of width len(neurons): an affine read-out of the neurons."""
    return bias + sum(g * eml_neuron(*n, x) for g, n in zip(out, neurons))


def sq_layer(h: float, x: float) -> float:
    """The width-2 central-difference squaring layer S_h(x) ~ x^2.

    Realised literally as an EML layer: neurons (h,0,0,1) and (-h,0,0,1),
    read-out weights 1/h^2 each, bias -2/h^2.
    """
    return eml_layer(
        neurons=((h, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0), (-h, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0)),
        out=(1.0 / h**2, 1.0 / h**2),
        bias=-2.0 / h**2,
        x=x,
    )


def forward_layer(h: float, x: float) -> float:
    """The width-1 forward-difference layer F_h(x) = 2(e^{hx} - 1 - hx)/h^2.

    The linear term is supplied by the affine read-out; this construction is
    only first order in h.
    """
    return 2.0 * (math.exp(h * x) - 1.0 - h * x) / h**2


def sq_layer_deriv(h: float, x: float) -> float:
    """Exact derivative of S_h:  (e^{hx} - e^{-hx})/h  ~  2x."""
    return (math.exp(h * x) - math.exp(-h * x)) / h


def prod_gate(h: float, x: float, y: float) -> float:
    """Width-4 polarisation gate  P_h(x,y) = (S_h(x+y) - S_h(x-y))/4  ~  x y."""
    return (sq_layer(h, x + y) - sq_layer(h, x - y)) / 4.0


def quad_form_network(h: float, A: Sequence[Sequence[float]], x: Sequence[float]) -> float:
    """Single EML layer of width <= 4 n^2 computing sum_{i,j} A_ij x_i x_j."""
    n = len(x)
    return sum(A[i][j] * prod_gate(h, x[i], x[j]) for i in range(n) for j in range(n))


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. The ReLU model
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def relu(t: float) -> float:
    return t if t > 0.0 else 0.0


def relu_net(
    a: Sequence[float],
    w: Sequence[float],
    b: Sequence[float],
    c0: float,
    c1: float,
    x: float,
) -> float:
    """One-hidden-layer ReLU network with a free affine skip connection."""
    return c0 + c1 * x + sum(ai * relu(wi * x + bi) for ai, wi, bi in zip(a, w, b))


def softplus(t: float) -> float:
    """Numerically stable log(1 + e^t)."""
    if t > 30.0:
        return t + math.log1p(math.exp(-t))
    return math.log1p(math.exp(t))

# 3. Utilities

def grid(n: int, lo: float = 0.0, hi: float = 1.0) -> List[float]:
    return [lo + (hi - lo) * i / n for i in range(n + 1)]


def sup_error(f: Callable[[float], float], g: Callable[[float], float], pts: Sequence[float]) -> float:
    return max(abs(f(t) - g(t)) for t in pts)

def piecewise_linear_relu_fit_error(k: int, m: int = 2000) -> float:
    """Uniform error of the interpolating k-unit shallow ReLU network on x^2.

    With k units (plus the affine skip connection) the network has k kinks and
    hence k+1 linear pieces.  Interpolating x^2 at the nodes j/(k+1) gives the
    per-piece chord error L^2/4 with L = 1/(k+1), i.e. 1/(4(k+1)^2); the
    Chebyshev-optimal piecewise fit halves this to 1/(8(k+1)^2).  Both sit
    above the proved universal floor 1/(32(k+1)^2), which therefore has the
    right exponent and is off only by a small constant factor.
    """
    pieces = k + 1
    nodes = [j / pieces for j in range(pieces + 1)]
    worst = 0.0
    for j in range(pieces):
        p, q = nodes[j], nodes[j + 1]
        for i in range(m // pieces + 1):
            x = p + (q - p) * i / (m // pieces + 1)
            interp = p * p + (x - p) * (p + q)   # chord through (p,p^2),(q,q^2)
            worst = max(worst, abs(x * x - interp))
    return worst

        # a random network, to illustrate that the floor is a *universal* bound
        a = [rng.uniform(-2, 2) for _ in range(k)]

    print("Mechanism: with k units there are at most k kinks, so one of the k+1")
    print("equal subintervals of [0,1] carries none and the network is exactly")

def demo_lipschitz_rate() -> None:
    banner("10. Lipschitz Jackson rate 2L/N for the interpolant (inherited by EML)")

    def f(x: float) -> float:                    # 1-Lipschitz sawtooth-ish target
        return abs(x - 0.5) + 0.3 * math.sin(2.0 * x)

    L = 1.0 + 0.6                                # |f'| <= 1 + 0.6
    pts = grid(2000)
    print(f"{'N':>5} {'max|f - interp|':>18} {'2L/N':>12} {'ratio':>8}")
    for N in (2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64):
        def interp(x: float, N: int = N) -> float:
            j = min(int(x * N), N - 1)
            p, q = j / N, (j + 1) / N
            t = (x - p) / (q - p)
            return (1 - t) * f(p) + t * f(q)

        print(f"{N:5d} {err:18.3e} {2 * L / N:12.3e} {err / (2 * L / N):8.4f}")
    print("The rate is Theta(1/N) for both models: on the raw Lipschitz class")
    print("smoothness gives no advantage.  The h^2 phenomenon is about smooth")
    print("targets, not about width.")

from __future__ import annotations

import math
import random
from itertools import product
from typing import Callable, List, Sequence, Tuple

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. The EML model
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def eml_neuron(a: float, b: float, c: float, d: float, x: float) -> float:
    """A single EML neuron:  x -> exp(a x + b) - log(c x + d).

    Setting c = 0, d = 1 switches the logarithmic branch off (log 1 = 0).
    """
    return math.exp(a * x + b) - math.log(c * x + d)


def eml_layer(
    neurons: Sequence[Tuple[float, float, float, float]],
    out: Sequence[float],
    bias: float,
    x: float,
) -> float:
    """An EML layer of width len(neurons): an affine read-out of the neurons."""
    return bias + sum(g * eml_neuron(*n, x) for g, n in zip(out, neurons))


def sq_layer(h: float, x: float) -> float:
    """The width-2 central-difference squaring layer S_h(x) ~ x^2.

    Realised literally as an EML layer: neurons (h,0,0,1) and (-h,0,0,1),
    read-out weights 1/h^2 each, bias -2/h^2.
    """
    return eml_layer(
        neurons=((h, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0), (-h, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0)),
        out=(1.0 / h**2, 1.0 / h**2),
        bias=-2.0 / h**2,
        x=x,
    )


def forward_layer(h: float, x: float) -> float:
    """The width-1 forward-difference layer F_h(x) = 2(e^{hx} - 1 - hx)/h^2.

    The linear term is supplied by the affine read-out; this construction is
    only first order in h.
    """
    return 2.0 * (math.exp(h * x) - 1.0 - h * x) / h**2


def sq_layer_deriv(h: float, x: float) -> float:
    """Exact derivative of S_h:  (e^{hx} - e^{-hx})/h  ~  2x."""
    return (math.exp(h * x) - math.exp(-h * x)) / h


def prod_gate(h: float, x: float, y: float) -> float:
    """Width-4 polarisation gate  P_h(x,y) = (S_h(x+y) - S_h(x-y))/4  ~  x y."""
    return (sq_layer(h, x + y) - sq_layer(h, x - y)) / 4.0


def quad_form_network(h: float, A: Sequence[Sequence[float]], x: Sequence[float]) -> float:
    """Single EML layer of width <= 4 n^2 computing sum_{i,j} A_ij x_i x_j."""
    n = len(x)
    return sum(A[i][j] * prod_gate(h, x[i], x[j]) for i in range(n) for j in range(n))


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. The ReLU model
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def relu(t: float) -> float:
    return t if t > 0.0 else 0.0


def relu_net(
    a: Sequence[float],
    w: Sequence[float],
    b: Sequence[float],
    c0: float,
    c1: float,
    x: float,
) -> float:
    """One-hidden-layer ReLU network with a free affine skip connection."""
    return c0 + c1 * x + sum(ai * relu(wi * x + bi) for ai, wi, bi in zip(a, w, b))


def softplus(t: float) -> float:
    """Numerically stable log(1 + e^t)."""
    if t > 30.0:
        return t + math.log1p(math.exp(-t))
    return math.log1p(math.exp(t))

# 3. Utilities
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def grid(n: int, lo: float = 0.0, hi: float = 1.0) -> List[float]:
    return [lo + (hi - lo) * i / n for i in range(n + 1)]


def sup_error(f: Callable[[float], float], g: Callable[[float], float], pts: Sequence[float]) -> float:
    return max(abs(f(t) - g(t)) for t in pts)

    hence k+1 linear pieces.  Interpolating x^2 at the nodes j/(k+1) gives the

    Chebyshev-optimal piecewise fit halves this to 1/(8(k+1)^2).  Both sit
    above the proved universal floor 1/(32(k+1)^2), which therefore has the
    right exponent and is off only by a small constant factor.
    """
    pieces = k + 1
    nodes = [j / pieces for j in range(pieces + 1)]
    worst = 0.0
    for j in range(pieces):
        p, q = nodes[j], nodes[j + 1]
        for i in range(m // pieces + 1):
            x = p + (q - p) * i / (m // pieces + 1)
            interp = p * p + (x - p) * (p + q)   # chord through (p,p^2),(q,q^2)
            worst = max(worst, abs(x * x - interp))
    return worst

from __future__ import annotations

import math
from typing import Callable, List, Tuple


def sq_layer(h: float, x: float) -> float:
    """Naive evaluation: (e^{hx} + e^{-hx} - 2)/h^2."""
    return (math.exp(h * x) + math.exp(-h * x) - 2.0) / h**2


def sq_layer_stable(h: float, x: float) -> float:
    """Stable evaluation.  e^u + e^{-u} - 2 = (e^{u/2} - e^{-u/2})^2, and the
    inner difference is computed with expm1 to avoid cancellation."""
    u = h * x / 2.0
    d = math.expm1(u) - math.expm1(-u)          # = e^{u} - e^{-u} without loss
    return d * d / h**2


def richardson(h: float, x: float,
               base: Callable[[float, float], float] = sq_layer_stable) -> float:
    """Fourth-order width-4 layer: (4 S_{h/2} - S_h)/3, cancelling the h^2 term."""
    return (4.0 * base(h / 2.0, x) - base(h, x)) / 3.0


def sup_error(f: Callable[[float], float], n: int = 400) -> float:
    return max(abs(f(i / n) - (i / n) ** 2) for i in range(n + 1))


def sweep(name: str, layer: Callable[[float, float], float]) -> Tuple[float, float]:
    print(f"\n{name}")
    print(f"{'h':>12} {'realised error':>16} {'truncation model':>18} "
          f"{'read-out 1/h^2':>15}")
    best: Tuple[float, float] = (float("inf"), 1.0)
    hs: List[float] = [10 ** (-t / 2) for t in range(0, 24)]
    for h in hs:
        err = sup_error(lambda x, h=h: layer(h, x))
        model = h**2 / 12.0
        if err < best[0]:
            best = (err, h)
        print(f"{h:12.2e} {err:16.3e} {model:18.3e} {1 / h**2:15.2e}")
    print(f"  -> best accuracy {best[0]:.3e} attained at h = {best[1]:.2e}")

from __future__ import annotations

import math
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import List, Tuple


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Neuron:
    """An EML neuron  x -> exp(a x + b) - log(c x + d)."""
    a: float
    b: float
    c: float
    d: float

    def __call__(self, x: float) -> float:
        return math.exp(self.a * x + self.b) - math.log(self.c * x + self.d)


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Layer:
    """An affine read-out of finitely many neurons."""
    neurons: Tuple[Neuron, ...]
    out: Tuple[float, ...]
    bias: float

    @property
    def width(self) -> int:
        return len(self.neurons)

    def __call__(self, x: float) -> float:
        return self.bias + sum(g * n(x) for g, n in zip(self.out, self.neurons))


def synthesise_square_layer(eps: float) -> Tuple[Layer, float, float]:
    """Return a width-2 layer with uniform error <= eps on x^2 over [0,1].

    The scale is h = min(1, sqrt(6 eps)), the two neurons are (h,0,0,1) and
    (-h,0,0,1) -- logarithmic branches switched off, since log 1 = 0 -- the
    read-out weights are 1/h^2 each and the bias is -2/h^2.  The guaranteed
    error is h^2/6 <= eps, and the price is the read-out magnitude 1/h^2.

    Returns (layer, h, guaranteed_error).
    """
    if eps <= 0.0:
        raise ValueError("eps must be positive")
    h = min(1.0, math.sqrt(6.0 * eps))
    layer = Layer(
        neurons=(Neuron(h, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0), Neuron(-h, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0)),
        out=(1.0 / h**2, 1.0 / h**2),
        bias=-2.0 / h**2,
    )
    return layer, h, h**2 / 6.0


def certify(layer: Layer, samples: int = 2000) -> float:
    """Empirical uniform error of `layer` against x^2 on [0,1]."""
    return max(abs(layer(i / samples) - (i / samples) ** 2) for i in range(samples + 1))

from __future__ import annotations

import math
from typing import List, Sequence, Tuple


def sq_layer(h: float, x: float) -> float:
    """Width-2 squaring layer  (e^{hx} + e^{-hx} - 2)/h^2  ~  x^2."""
    return (math.exp(h * x) + math.exp(-h * x) - 2.0) / h**2


def prod_gate(h: float, x: float, y: float) -> float:
    """Width-4 polarisation gate  (S_h(x+y) - S_h(x-y))/4  ~  x y."""
    return (sq_layer(h, x + y) - sq_layer(h, x - y)) / 4.0


def compile_quadratic_form(
    A: Sequence[Sequence[float]], eps: float
) -> Tuple[float, int, float]:
    """Choose the scale for a quadratic-form layer of the prescribed accuracy.

    For a coefficient matrix A the network  sum_{i,j} A_ij P_h(x_i, x_j)  has
    uniform error at most  h^2 * sum_{i,j} |A_ij|  on [0,1]^n, provided
    0 < h <= 1/2.  Setting h = min(1/2, sqrt(eps / ||A||_1)) therefore meets the
    target.  The layer has width at most 4 n^2 (four exponential neurons per
    monomial) and evaluation costs O(n^2) transcendental calls.

    Returns (h, width, guaranteed_error).
    """
    n = len(A)
    mass = sum(abs(A[i][j]) for i in range(n) for j in range(n))
    if mass == 0.0:
        return 0.5, 0, 0.0
    h = min(0.5, math.sqrt(eps / mass))
    return h, 4 * n * n, h**2 * mass


def evaluate(A: Sequence[Sequence[float]], x: Sequence[float], h: float) -> float:
    """Evaluate the compiled layer at the point x in [0,1]^n."""
    n = len(x)
    return sum(A[i][j] * prod_gate(h, x[i], x[j]) for i in range(n) for j in range(n))


def exact(A: Sequence[Sequence[float]], x: Sequence[float]) -> float:
    n = len(x)
    return sum(A[i][j] * x[i] * x[j] for i in range(n) for j in range(n))

def relu(t: float) -> float:
    return t if t > 0.0 else 0.0


def relu_net(a: Sequence[float], w: Sequence[float], b: Sequence[float],
             c0: float, c1: float, x: float) -> float:
    """One-hidden-layer rectified network with a free affine skip connection."""
    return c0 + c1 * x + sum(ai * relu(wi * x + bi) for ai, wi, bi in zip(a, w, b))


def affine_window(w: Sequence[float], b: Sequence[float]) -> Tuple[float, float]:
    """Return a breakpoint-free subinterval of [0,1] of length 1/(k+1).

    A unit with w_i != 0 has exactly one breakpoint -b_i/w_i; a unit with
    w_i = 0 is constant and has none.  At most k points cannot meet all k+1
    equal subintervals of [0,1], so some subinterval is free of them and the
    whole network is exactly affine there.  Cost: O(k^2) in the naive form
    below, O(k log k) if the breakpoints are sorted first.
    """
    k = len(w)
    breaks: List[float] = [-bi / wi for wi, bi in zip(w, b) if wi != 0.0]
    for j in range(k + 1):
        p, q = j / (k + 1), (j + 1) / (k + 1)
        if not any(p < t < q for t in breaks):
            return p, q
    raise RuntimeError("pigeonhole principle cannot fail")


def certified_lower_bound(
    a: Sequence[float], w: Sequence[float], b: Sequence[float], c0: float, c1: float
) -> Tuple[float, float, float, float]:
    """Certify that the network errs by at least L^2/32 on x^2.

    Returns (p, q, proved_floor, witnessed_error), where (p,q) is the
    breakpoint-free window, proved_floor = (q-p)^2/32 = 1/(32(k+1)^2), and
    witnessed_error is the largest of the three quarter-point deviations that
    the second-difference argument uses.
    """
    p, q = affine_window(w, b)
    L = q - p
    xs = (p + L / 4, p + L / 2, p + 3 * L / 4)
    witnessed = max(abs(x * x - relu_net(a, w, b, c0, c1, x)) for x in xs)
    return p, q, L * L / 32.0, witnessed

from __future__ import annotations

import math
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import List, Sequence, Tuple


def relu(t: float) -> float:
    return t if t > 0.0 else 0.0


def softplus(t: float) -> float:
    """Numerically stable log(1 + e^t)."""
    return t + math.log1p(math.exp(-t)) if t > 30.0 else math.log1p(math.exp(t))


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Chain:
    """One depth-2 chain: x -> exp(a x + b), then u -> -log(c u + d), read out.

    With (a, b) = (M w, M b) in the first neuron and (c, d) = (1, 1) in the
    second, the chain computes -log(1 + e^{M(w x + b)}) = -softplus(M(w x + b)),
    which the read-out weight -a/M turns into a * softplus(M(w x + b))/M.
    """
    w: float
    b: float
    scale: float          # the inner scale M
    out: float            # the read-out weight a_i

    def __call__(self, x: float) -> float:
        return self.out * softplus(self.scale * (self.w * x + self.b)) / self.scale


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Depth2Net:
    chains: Tuple[Chain, ...]
    skip0: float
    skip1: float

    @property
    def width(self) -> int:
        return len(self.chains)

    def __call__(self, x: float) -> float:
        return self.skip0 + self.skip1 * x + sum(ch(x) for ch in self.chains)


def emulate(
    a: Sequence[float], w: Sequence[float], b: Sequence[float],
    c0: float, c1: float, delta: float,
) -> Tuple[Depth2Net, float]:
    """Build a depth-2 network within `delta` of the given rectified network.

    Since |M^{-1} log(1 + e^{Mt}) - relu(t)| <= log 2 / M for every t, summing
    over the units gives an emulation error at most (sum_i |a_i|) log 2 / M,
    uniformly on the whole real line.  Choosing
        M = max(1, (sum_i |a_i|) log 2 / delta)
    meets the target.  Width and depth are unchanged: k chains, depth 2.

    Returns (network, guaranteed_error).
    """
    mass = sum(abs(ai) for ai in a)
    M = max(1.0, mass * math.log(2.0) / delta) if delta > 0 else 1.0
    chains = tuple(Chain(wi, bi, M, ai) for ai, wi, bi in zip(a, w, b))
    return Depth2Net(chains, c0, c1), mass * math.log(2.0) / M

### A guided tour of the depth–width–precision trade-off, starting from the humblest curve there is

---

## 0. The question, in one picture

Build a network that computes $x^2$ on $[0,1]$.

That is the whole problem. No high dimensions, no noise, no adversary — just a parabola. And it is already enough to separate two families of neural networks by a *polynomial* factor in their width. By the end of this page you will know exactly why, and you will have watched it happen.

Here is the experiment in full. On the left, a **width-2 smooth layer**; on the right, the best **polyline** a one-hidden-layer rectified network can produce. Drag the two sliders and watch which error falls faster.

{{interactive_demo:0}}

Three things are worth noticing before we explain anything:

1. The green curve's error falls like $h^2$ **without the width ever changing**. Two neurons, forever.
2. The orange curve's error also falls like a square — but of $1/(k+1)$, so you must *buy neurons* to get it.
3. The purple dashed line is a **floor**: a level no rectified network with $k$ units can go below, whatever its parameters. That is a theorem, not an observation.

---

## 1. Why a polyline cannot follow a parabola

Let us start with the negative result, because it is the more surprising one and its proof is completely elementary.

A one-hidden-layer rectified network with $k$ units is
$$R(x) = c_0 + c_1 x + \sum_{i=1}^{k} a_i \,\mathrm{relu}(w_i x + b_i), \qquad \mathrm{relu}(t)=\max(t,0),$$
with arbitrary real parameters — and we generously grant the affine term $c_0+c_1x$ for free. Every such $R$ is **piecewise linear**: unit $i$ contributes at most one kink, at $x = -b_i/w_i$.

<details>
<summary><b>Click to reveal the full proof of the lower bound</b> (pigeonhole + a three-point second difference)</summary>

**Step 1 — pigeonhole.** Cut $[0,1]$ into the $k+1$ equal open intervals $I_j = \big(\tfrac{j}{k+1}, \tfrac{j+1}{k+1}\big)$. There are at most $k$ kinks (units with $w_i = 0$ contribute none — they are constants), so at least one $I_j$ contains no kink at all.

**Step 2 — exact affinity.** On such an interval each expression $w_ix+b_i$ has constant sign, so $\mathrm{relu}(w_ix+b_i)$ equals either $w_ix+b_i$ throughout or $0$ throughout. Summing, there are reals $\alpha,\beta$ with
$$R(x) = \alpha x + \beta \quad \text{for all } x \in I_j.$$
Not "approximately affine" — *exactly* affine.

**Step 3 — a line cannot follow a parabola.** Let $L = 1/(k+1)$ be the length of $I_j = (p, p+L)$ and evaluate at the three points $x_1 = p+\tfrac{L}{4}$, $x_2 = p+\tfrac{L}{2}$, $x_3 = p+\tfrac{3L}{4}$. The second-difference functional
$$g \;\longmapsto\; g(x_1) - 2g(x_2) + g(x_3)$$
kills every affine function and sends $x^2$ to $2(L/4)^2 = L^2/8$. Hence if $|x^2 - R(x)| \le \varepsilon$ on $I_j$ then
$$\frac{L^2}{8} \;=\; \big(x_1^2 - R(x_1)\big) - 2\big(x_2^2 - R(x_2)\big) + \big(x_3^2 - R(x_3)\big) \;\le\; 4\varepsilon .$$

**Conclusion.** $\varepsilon \ge L^2/32 = \dfrac{1}{32(k+1)^2}$. $\blacksquare$

*(The optimal constant here is $1/8$, from the endpoints; $1/32$ is the price of sampling interior points, which keeps the argument valid on an open interval. Only the exponent matters for what follows.)*

</details>

> **Theorem (shallow rectified barrier).** For every $k$ and every choice of parameters,
> $$\max_{0\le x\le 1}\big|x^2 - R(x)\big| \;\ge\; \frac{1}{32(k+1)^2}.$$

The same argument bites on *slopes*: on the empty window the network's slope is a single number $\alpha$, while $2x$ sweeps a range of width $2/(k+1)$, so somewhere $|\alpha - 2x| \ge \tfrac{1}{2(k+1)}$. Rectified gradients are only **first order** in the width.

## 2. Now change the neuron

An **EML neuron** — exponential minus logarithm — computes
$$x \;\longmapsto\; e^{ax+b} - \log(cx+d),$$
and a **layer of width $k$** is an affine read-out of $k$ of them. Take just two, both with the logarithmic branch switched off ($c=0$, $d=1$, so $\log 1 = 0$), with inner weights $+h$ and $-h$, read-out weights $1/h^2$ each and bias $-2/h^2$:
$$\boxed{\;S_h(x) \;=\; \frac{e^{hx} + e^{-hx} - 2}{h^2}\;}$$

This is the second central difference of the exponential, i.e. $\tfrac{2}{h^2}\big(\cosh(hx)-1\big)$, and its Taylor series is
$$S_h(x) \;=\; x^2 \;+\; \frac{h^2x^4}{12} \;+\; \frac{h^4x^6}{360} \;+\; \cdots$$
Every term after the first carries $h^2$. That is the entire idea.

> **Theorem (second-order squaring at width two).** If $|hx| \le 1$ then $\big|S_h(x) - x^2\big| \le \dfrac{h^2x^4}{6}$; in particular the uniform error on $[0,1]$ is at most $h^2/6$, and it is at least $h^2/14$ at $x = 1$. The rate is exactly $\Theta(h^2)$, at **constant width 2**.

<details>
<summary><b>Click to reveal the proof</b> (a controlled Taylor remainder, both directions)</summary>

*Upper bound.* Write $u = hx$. Expanding $e^{u}$ and $e^{-u}$ to fifth order (legitimate since $|u|\le1$), all **odd** powers cancel in the sum $e^u + e^{-u}$; subtracting $2 + u^2$ leaves the quartic term $2u^4/4! = u^4/12$ plus fifth-order remainders bounded by an explicit constant times $|u|^5 \le u^4$. Collecting, $\big|e^u+e^{-u}-2-u^2\big| \le u^4/6$. Dividing by $h^2$ and substituting $u = hx$ gives the claim. The asymptotic constant is $1/12$; the factor two is the price of a bound valid uniformly on the whole range.

*Lower bound.* Partial sums of the exponential series underestimate $e^h$ for $h \ge 0$; combining that with a two-sided remainder estimate for $e^{-h}$ and absorbing the $h^5, h^6$ terms into $h^4$ (using $h\le1$) gives $e^h + e^{-h} \ge 2 + h^2 + h^4/14$. Evaluating at $x=1$, $S_h(1)-1 = \big(e^h+e^{-h}-2-h^2\big)/h^2 \ge h^2/14$. $\blacksquare$

</details>

Compare: **any** accuracy $\varepsilon$ is reached at width $2$ (take $h = \min(1,\varepsilon)$), while a rectified network needs $(k+1)^2 \ge 1/(32\varepsilon)$, that is, width $\Omega(\varepsilon^{-1/2})$.

The convergence portrait puts the two laws side by side on log–log axes:

<details>
<summary><b>Wait — isn't this cheating?</b> (the honest caveat about weight magnitude)</summary>

It is not cheating, but it *is* a trade. The read-out weights are $\pm 1/h^2$, and the two exponentials very nearly cancel: at accuracy $\varepsilon = h^2/6$ the coefficients have magnitude about $1/(6\varepsilon)$. So the correct slogan is not "smooth activations need fewer neurons" but:

> **width, depth and weight magnitude are three currencies; an analytic activation can pay in any of them, a piecewise-linear one can pay only in width.**

This has a real numerical consequence, which you can watch in Section 6: in double precision the naive evaluation stalls near $10^{-8}$, exactly the $\sqrt{u}$ floor of central differencing. And it has a real theoretical consequence: under a *bounded-weight* budget the separation would have to be re-proved. That is the first open problem on the list at the end.

</details>

---

## 3. Gradients come along for free

Differentiating $S_h$ gives $\big(e^{hx}-e^{-hx}\big)/h$, the central difference for $\sinh$, and the same cancellation of even powers applies:

> **Theorem.** For $0 < h \le 1$ and $x \in [0,1]$: $\left|\dfrac{e^{hx}-e^{-hx}}{h} - 2x\right| \le \dfrac{h^2}{2}$.

The *same two neurons*, with no retraining, track the derivative to second order — against the rectified network's $\Omega(1/k)$. Whenever the derivative of the learned function is the object of interest (physics-informed models, sensitivity analysis, control, calibration), this is the more consequential half of the story.

---

## 4. Depth multiplies the degree

If $S_h(x) \approx x^2$, then $S_h(S_h(x))$ should be about $x^4$ — provided the intermediate value stays inside the regime where the estimate holds.

> **Theorem (depth 2).** For $0 < h \le 1/2$ and $x\in[0,1]$: $\big|S_h(S_h(x)) - x^4\big| \le h^2$.

<details>
<summary><b>Click to reveal the proof</b> — and the stability invariant that makes depth safe</summary>

Put $y = S_h(x)$ and split
$$S_h(S_h(x)) - x^4 = \underbrace{\big(S_h(y) - y^2\big)}_{\text{layer 2's own error}} + \underbrace{\big(y^2 - x^4\big)}_{\text{propagated error}}.$$

*Stability.* From $|y - x^2| \le h^2/6 \le 1/24$ and $0\le x^2\le1$ we get $|y| \le 25/24$, hence $|hy| \le \tfrac12\cdot\tfrac{25}{24} < 1$ — exactly the hypothesis under which the second-order estimate may be applied at the point $y$. This is the *only* use of $h\le 1/2$, and it is the whole mechanism by which depth composes.

*First term.* $|S_h(y)-y^2| \le h^2y^4/6 \le h^2/3$, since $y^4 \le (25/24)^4 \le 2$.

*Second term.* $y^2 - x^4 = (y-x^2)(y+x^2)$ with $|y+x^2| \le 25/24+1$, so it is at most $\tfrac{h^2}{6}\cdot\tfrac{49}{24}\le h^2/2$.

Adding, $h^2/3 + h^2/2 \le h^2$. $\blacksquare$

</details>

Four neurons in total (two layers of two), a degree-four target at second order. The conjecture — depth $m$ gives $x^{2^m}$ at constant width with a constant growing like $2^m$ — is stated at the end; the induction hinges on precisely the invariant above.

---

## 5. Polarisation: four neurons that multiply

One classical identity turns a squarer into a multiplier:
$$xy = \frac{(x+y)^2 - (x-y)^2}{4}.$$
Feed the two-neuron layer the pre-activations $x+y$ and $x-y$ and combine:
$$P_h(x,y) = \frac{S_h(x+y) - S_h(x-y)}{4}.$$

That is **four** neurons, and its error on the unit square is again exactly quadratic: at most $h^2$ everywhere, at least $2h^2/7$ at the corner $(1,1)$.

Explore the error surface, and then slide the dimension to see the payoff:

{{interactive_demo:1}}

> **Theorem (quadratic forms).** For $A \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$, $q(x)=\sum_{i,j}A_{ij}x_ix_j$ and $0<h\le\tfrac12$,
> $$\left|\sum_{i,j}A_{ij}P_h(x_i,x_j) - q(x)\right| \;\le\; h^2\sum_{i,j}|A_{ij}| \qquad \text{on } [0,1]^n,$$
> and the left-hand side is a **single** layer of width at most $4n^2$.

The constant $h^2$ is *dimension-free*: the ambient dimension enters only through the coefficient mass. Meanwhile the rectified barrier survives the passage to two inputs at zero cost — restricting a bivariate network to the diagonal $y=x$ turns $\mathrm{relu}(w_ix+v_iy+b_i)$ into $\mathrm{relu}((w_i+v_i)x+b_i)$ and $xy$ into $x^2$, so the same $1/(32(k+1)^2)$ floor applies to the product.

## 6. The catch, measured

Everything above is exact mathematics in exact arithmetic. In floating point, the near-cancellation in $e^{hx}+e^{-hx}-2$ meets the division by $h^2$, and the realised error behaves like
$$\underbrace{\frac{h^2}{12}}_{\text{truncation}} \;+\; \underbrace{\frac{C\,u}{h^2}}_{\text{cancellation}},$$
minimised at $h \sim u^{1/4}$ with a floor of order $\sqrt{u}$ — the classical trade-off of central differencing. This demo measures it, and then shows two remedies: a stably evaluated form, and Richardson extrapolation across two scales, $R_h = (4S_{h/2}-S_h)/3$, which cancels the $h^2$ term and gives a **fourth-order width-4 layer** reaching a given accuracy at a much larger (hence much safer) $h$.

{{demo:1}}

## 7. The other direction: smooth is never worse

A separation theorem is only half a story. Could the smooth model be *bad* at kinks, at corners, at non-smooth targets?

No — and for a charming structural reason. **Softplus is an EML composite**: $\mathrm{softplus}(t) = \log(1+e^{t})$ is an exponential neuron feeding a logarithmic one, i.e. exactly a depth-2 chain. And it approximates the rectifier uniformly after rescaling:
$$\left|\frac{\log(1+e^{Mt})}{M} - \mathrm{relu}(t)\right| \;\le\; \frac{\log 2}{M}\quad\text{for all }t,$$
with equality at $t=0$, where the smooth curve rounds the corner by exactly $\log 2/M$.

{{visualization:2}}

<details>
<summary><b>Click to reveal the proof and its consequence</b></summary>

*Two elementary inequalities.* $\mathrm{relu}(t) \le \mathrm{softplus}(t) \le \mathrm{relu}(t) + \log 2$: for $t\le0$ both sides are between $0$ and $\log 2$; for $t>0$ write $\log(1+e^t) = t + \log(1+e^{-t})$ and note $0 < \log(1+e^{-t}) \le \log 2$. Apply this at $Mt$, use $\mathrm{relu}(Mt) = M\,\mathrm{relu}(t)$, divide by $M$.

*Emulation.* Summing over $k$ units, a depth-2 network with $k$ chains reproduces any $k$-unit rectified network to within $\big(\sum_i|a_i|\big)\log2/M$, uniformly on the whole line — and $M$ is ours to choose.

*Consequence (Jackson rate).* The piecewise-linear interpolant of an $L$-Lipschitz $f$ at the nodes $j/N$ is a width-$N$ rectified network (read-out weights = slope jumps) with error $\le 2L/N$. Emulating it gives: for every $N\ge1$ and $\delta>0$ there is a depth-2 smooth network with $N$ chains and uniform error at most $2L/N+\delta$. $\blacksquare$

</details>

## 8. What the two rates mean together

Put the halves side by side:

| target class | smooth model | shallow rectified model |
|---|---|---|
| $L$-Lipschitz on $[0,1]$ | $2L/N + \delta$ at width $N$ (depth 2) | $2L/N$ at width $N$ |
| $x^2$ on $[0,1]$ | $\Theta(h^2)$ at width **2** | $\Theta((k+1)^{-2})$, never below $\tfrac{1}{32(k+1)^2}$ |
| derivative $2x$ | $O(h^2)$ at width **2** | $\Omega(1/k)$ |
| $xy$ on $[0,1]^2$ | $\Theta(h^2)$ at width **4** | never below $\tfrac{1}{32(k+1)^2}$ |
| quadratic form in $n$ vars | $h^2\sum_{i,j}|A_{ij}|$ at width $4n^2$ | $\Omega(k^{-2})$ already for $n=2$ |

The conclusion is sharper than the usual slogan. The famous "$O(w^{-2})$ rate" is **not** a statement about width: on the raw Lipschitz class both models sit at $\Theta(1/N)$, because a Lipschitz function has no second derivative to exploit. On smooth targets the smooth model gets $\Theta(h^2)$ at *constant* width, paying in precision instead. **Smoothness of the activation buys you the right to spend precision instead of neurons.**

## 9. Where this goes

**Bounded weights.** Cap all weights at $W$. Conjecture: accuracy $\varepsilon$ then costs width $k \gtrsim \varepsilon^{-1/2}/\log W$, so under a polynomial weight budget the polynomial separation softens to a logarithmic one. The pigeonhole argument of Section 1 is the template: under a weight cap, a smooth layer also has a bounded number of effective "pieces".

**Depth as a degree multiplier.** $S_h^{\circ m} \approx x^{2^m}$ with error $\le 2^m h^2$, at constant width — proved for $m=2$, and the stability invariant of Section 4 is exactly the induction hypothesis.

**Beyond quadratics.** Products give monomials, monomials give polynomials. Which polynomial classes admit width polynomial in the degree with dimension-free constants? What replaces the coefficient mass — a Barron-type norm?

**Optimisation.** Every result here is about *expressivity*: good parameters exist. Whether gradient descent finds a delicate near-cancellation of two large exponentials is a different, and genuinely open, question — and the honest counterweight to all of the above.

import Mathlib

namespace EML.SoftplusJackson

open Real Set

noncomputable section

/-! ## Definitions shared with `EMLDepthWidthTradeoff` -/

/-- ReLU. -/
def relu (t : ℝ) : ℝ := max t 0

/-- A one-hidden-layer ReLU network with `k` units and an affine skip connection. -/
def reluNet (k : ℕ) (a w b : Fin k → ℝ) (c₀ c₁ : ℝ) (x : ℝ) : ℝ :=
  c₀ + c₁ * x + ∑ i, a i * relu (w i * x + b i)

/-- Parameters of a single EML neuron `x ↦ exp(a x + b) − log(c x + d)`. -/
structure Neuron where
  /-- weight inside the exponential branch -/
  a : ℝ
  /-- bias inside the exponential branch -/
  b : ℝ
  /-- weight inside the logarithmic branch -/
  c : ℝ
  /-- bias inside the logarithmic branch -/
  d : ℝ

/-- The function computed by an EML neuron. -/
def Neuron.eval (N : Neuron) (x : ℝ) : ℝ :=
  Real.exp (N.a * x + N.b) - Real.log (N.c * x + N.d)

/-! ## Softplus and the emulation of ReLU networks -/

/-- Softplus `t ↦ log (1 + exp t)`. -/
def softplus (t : ℝ) : ℝ := Real.log (1 + Real.exp t)

theorem relu_le_softplus (t : ℝ) : relu t ≤ softplus t := by
  have hexp : (0:ℝ) < Real.exp t := Real.exp_pos t
  rcases le_or_gt t 0 with ht | ht
  · have : relu t = 0 := by simp [relu, max_eq_right ht]
    rw [this, softplus]
    have : (1:ℝ) ≤ 1 + Real.exp t := by linarith
    simpa using Real.log_nonneg this
  · have hr : relu t = t := by simp [relu, max_eq_left ht.le]
    rw [hr, softplus]
    have h1 : Real.exp t ≤ 1 + Real.exp t := by linarith
    calc t = Real.log (Real.exp t) := (Real.log_exp t).symm
      _ ≤ Real.log (1 + Real.exp t) := Real.log_le_log hexp h1

theorem softplus_le_relu_add_log_two (t : ℝ) : softplus t ≤ relu t + Real.log 2 := by
  have hexp : (0:ℝ) < Real.exp t := Real.exp_pos t
  rcases le_or_gt t 0 with ht | ht
  · have hr : relu t = 0 := by simp [relu, max_eq_right ht]
    rw [hr, softplus, zero_add]
    have h1 : 1 + Real.exp t ≤ 2 := by
      have : Real.exp t ≤ 1 := by
        simpa using Real.exp_le_exp.2 ht
      linarith
    exact Real.log_le_log (by linarith) h1
  · have hr : relu t = t := by simp [relu, max_eq_left ht.le]
    rw [hr, softplus]
    have hid : 1 + Real.exp t = Real.exp t * (1 + Real.exp (-t)) := by
      rw [mul_add, mul_one, ← Real.exp_add, add_neg_cancel, Real.exp_zero]
      ring
    rw [hid, Real.log_mul (ne_of_gt hexp) (by positivity), Real.log_exp]
    have h1 : 1 + Real.exp (-t) ≤ 2 := by
      have : Real.exp (-t) ≤ 1 := by
        simpa using Real.exp_le_exp.2 (by linarith : -t ≤ 0)
      linarith
    have := Real.log_le_log (by positivity : (0:ℝ) < 1 + Real.exp (-t)) h1
    linarith

/-- The scaled softplus is a two-sided `log 2 / M`-approximation of ReLU. -/
theorem scaled_softplus_approx_relu (M t : ℝ) (hM : 0 < M) :
    |softplus (M * t) / M - relu t| ≤ Real.log 2 / M := by
  have h1 := relu_le_softplus (M * t)
  have h2 := softplus_le_relu_add_log_two (M * t)
  have hscale : relu (M * t) = M * relu t := by
    simp [relu, mul_max_of_nonneg _ _ hM.le]
  rw [hscale] at h1 h2
  have key : softplus (M * t) / M - relu t = (softplus (M * t) - M * relu t) / M := by
    field_simp
  rw [key, abs_div, abs_of_pos hM]
  gcongr
  rw [abs_le]
  constructor <;> linarith

/-! ## Depth-2 EML networks with parallel chains -/

/-- A **depth-2 EML network**: `k` parallel chains, each an EML neuron of the
second layer applied to the output of an EML neuron of the first layer, together
with an affine read-out and an affine skip connection. -/
structure Depth2Net (k : ℕ) where
  /-- neurons of the first layer -/
  first : Fin k → Neuron
  /-- neurons of the second layer -/
  second : Fin k → Neuron
  /-- read-out weights -/
  out : Fin k → ℝ
  /-- constant term of the skip connection -/
  skip0 : ℝ
  /-- linear term of the skip connection -/
  skip1 : ℝ

def Depth2Net.eval {k : ℕ} (N : Depth2Net k) (x : ℝ) : ℝ :=
  N.skip0 + N.skip1 * x + ∑ i, N.out i * (N.second i).eval ((N.first i).eval x)

/-- The depth-2 EML network that emulates a shallow ReLU network: the first layer
computes `exp (M (wᵢ x + bᵢ))`, the second layer applies `u ↦ 1 - log (1 + u)`,
which is exactly a (rescaled) softplus. -/
def softplusEmulator (k : ℕ) (a w b : Fin k → ℝ) (c₀ c₁ M : ℝ) : Depth2Net k where
  first i := ⟨M * w i, M * b i, 0, 1⟩
  second _ := ⟨0, 0, 1, 1⟩
  out i := -(a i) / M
  skip0 := c₀ + ∑ i, a i / M
  skip1 := c₁

theorem softplusEmulator_chain (k : ℕ) (a w b : Fin k → ℝ) (c₀ c₁ M : ℝ) (x : ℝ) (i : Fin k) :
    ((softplusEmulator k a w b c₀ c₁ M).second i).eval
        (((softplusEmulator k a w b c₀ c₁ M).first i).eval x)
      = 1 - softplus (M * (w i * x + b i)) := by
  simp only [softplusEmulator, Neuron.eval, softplus, zero_mul, zero_add,
    Real.exp_zero, one_mul, Real.log_one, sub_zero]
  rw [show M * w i * x + M * b i = M * (w i * x + b i) by ring,
      show Real.exp (M * (w i * x + b i)) + 1 = 1 + Real.exp (M * (w i * x + b i)) by ring]

theorem softplusEmulator_eval (k : ℕ) (a w b : Fin k → ℝ) (c₀ c₁ M : ℝ) (hM : M ≠ 0) (x : ℝ) :
    (softplusEmulator k a w b c₀ c₁ M).eval x
      = c₀ + c₁ * x + ∑ i, a i * (softplus (M * (w i * x + b i)) / M) := by
  have hterm : ∀ i : Fin k,
      (softplusEmulator k a w b c₀ c₁ M).out i *
        ((softplusEmulator k a w b c₀ c₁ M).second i).eval
          (((softplusEmulator k a w b c₀ c₁ M).first i).eval x)
      = a i * (softplus (M * (w i * x + b i)) / M) - a i / M := by
    intro i
    rw [softplusEmulator_chain]
    show -(a i) / M * (1 - softplus (M * (w i * x + b i))) = _
    field_simp
    ring
  simp only [Depth2Net.eval]
  rw [Finset.sum_congr rfl (fun i _ => hterm i), Finset.sum_sub_distrib]
  show c₀ + ∑ i, a i / M + c₁ * x + _ = _
  ring

/-- **Depth-2 EML networks emulate shallow ReLU networks.**  With inner scale `M`
the emulation error is at most `(Σ |aᵢ|) log 2 / M`, uniformly on `ℝ`. -/
theorem softplusEmulator_error (k : ℕ) (a w b : Fin k → ℝ) (c₀ c₁ M : ℝ) (hM : 0 < M) (x : ℝ) :
    |(softplusEmulator k a w b c₀ c₁ M).eval x - reluNet k a w b c₀ c₁ x|
      ≤ (∑ i, |a i|) * (Real.log 2 / M) := by
  rw [softplusEmulator_eval k a w b c₀ c₁ M hM.ne' x, reluNet]
  have hdiff : c₀ + c₁ * x + ∑ i, a i * (softplus (M * (w i * x + b i)) / M)
      - (c₀ + c₁ * x + ∑ i, a i * relu (w i * x + b i))
      = ∑ i, a i * (softplus (M * (w i * x + b i)) / M - relu (w i * x + b i)) := by
    simp only [mul_sub, Finset.sum_sub_distrib]
    ring
  rw [hdiff]
  calc |∑ i, a i * (softplus (M * (w i * x + b i)) / M - relu (w i * x + b i))|
      ≤ ∑ i, |a i * (softplus (M * (w i * x + b i)) / M - relu (w i * x + b i))| :=
        Finset.abs_sum_le_sum_abs _ _
    _ ≤ ∑ i, |a i| * (Real.log 2 / M) := by
        refine Finset.sum_le_sum (fun i _ => ?_)
        rw [abs_mul]
        exact mul_le_mul_of_nonneg_left (scaled_softplus_approx_relu M _ hM) (abs_nonneg _)
    _ = (∑ i, |a i|) * (Real.log 2 / M) := by rw [Finset.sum_mul]

/-- **Depth-2 EML dominates shallow ReLU.**  Any function approximated to `ε` by a
`k`-unit shallow ReLU network on a set `S` is approximated to `ε + δ` by a
depth-2 EML network with `k` chains, for every `δ > 0`. -/
theorem emlDepth2_dominates_relu (k : ℕ) (a w b : Fin k → ℝ) (c₀ c₁ : ℝ)
    (f : ℝ → ℝ) (S : Set ℝ) (ε δ : ℝ) (hδ : 0 < δ)
    (h : ∀ x ∈ S, |f x - reluNet k a w b c₀ c₁ x| ≤ ε) :
    ∃ N : Depth2Net k, ∀ x ∈ S, |f x - N.eval x| ≤ ε + δ := by
  set A := ∑ i, |a i| with hA
  have hA0 : 0 ≤ A := Finset.sum_nonneg (fun i _ => abs_nonneg _)
  set M := max 1 (A * Real.log 2 / δ) with hMdef
  have hM : 0 < M := lt_of_lt_of_le one_pos (le_max_left _ _)
  refine ⟨softplusEmulator k a w b c₀ c₁ M, fun x hx => ?_⟩
  have h1 := softplusEmulator_error k a w b c₀ c₁ M hM x
  have h2 : A * (Real.log 2 / M) ≤ δ := by
    rw [mul_div_assoc'] at h1 ⊢
    rw [div_le_iff₀ hM]
    have : A * Real.log 2 / δ ≤ M := le_max_right _ _
    rw [div_le_iff₀ hδ] at this
    linarith
  calc |f x - (softplusEmulator k a w b c₀ c₁ M).eval x|
      ≤ |f x - reluNet k a w b c₀ c₁ x|
        + |reluNet k a w b c₀ c₁ x - (softplusEmulator k a w b c₀ c₁ M).eval x| := by
        have := abs_add_le (f x - reluNet k a w b c₀ c₁ x)
          (reluNet k a w b c₀ c₁ x - (softplusEmulator k a w b c₀ c₁ M).eval x)
        simpa using this
    _ ≤ ε + δ := by
        have h3 : |reluNet k a w b c₀ c₁ x - (softplusEmulator k a w b c₀ c₁ M).eval x|
            = |(softplusEmulator k a w b c₀ c₁ M).eval x - reluNet k a w b c₀ c₁ x| :=
          abs_sub_comm _ _
        rw [h3]
        linarith [h x hx, h1, h2]


/-! ## Piecewise-linear interpolation and the Lipschitz rate -/

/-- Slope of the linear interpolant of `f` on the `j`-th piece of the uniform
`N`-partition of `[0,1]`. -/
def interpSlope (f : ℝ → ℝ) (N : ℕ) (j : ℕ) : ℝ :=
  (f (((j : ℝ) + 1) / N) - f ((j : ℝ) / N)) * N

/-- The read-out weight attached to the breakpoint `j/N`: the jump of the slope. -/
def interpCoeff (f : ℝ → ℝ) (N : ℕ) (j : ℕ) : ℝ :=
  if j = 0 then interpSlope f N 0 else interpSlope f N j - interpSlope f N (j - 1)

/-- The ReLU network of width `N` realising the piecewise-linear interpolant of
`f` at the nodes `0, 1/N, …, 1`. -/
def lipReluNet (f : ℝ → ℝ) (N : ℕ) (x : ℝ) : ℝ :=
  reluNet N (fun i => interpCoeff f N (i : ℕ)) (fun _ => 1)
    (fun i => -((i : ℕ) : ℝ) / N) (f 0) 0 x

theorem sum_interpCoeff (f : ℝ → ℝ) (N j : ℕ) :
    ∑ i ∈ Finset.range (j + 1), interpCoeff f N i = interpSlope f N j := by
  induction j with
  | zero => simp [interpCoeff]
  | succ j ih =>
      rw [Finset.sum_range_succ, ih]
      simp [interpCoeff]

theorem sum_index_interpCoeff (f : ℝ → ℝ) (N j : ℕ) :
    ∑ i ∈ Finset.range (j + 1), (i : ℝ) * interpCoeff f N i
      = (j : ℝ) * interpSlope f N j - ∑ i ∈ Finset.range j, interpSlope f N i := by
  induction j with
  | zero => simp [interpCoeff]
  | succ j ih =>
      rw [Finset.sum_range_succ, ih, Finset.sum_range_succ]
      have hc : interpCoeff f N (j + 1) = interpSlope f N (j + 1) - interpSlope f N j := by
        simp [interpCoeff]
      rw [hc]
      push_cast
      ring

theorem sum_interpSlope (f : ℝ → ℝ) (N j : ℕ) :
    ∑ i ∈ Finset.range j, interpSlope f N i = (f ((j : ℝ) / N) - f 0) * N := by
  induction j with
  | zero => simp
  | succ j ih =>
      rw [Finset.sum_range_succ, ih, interpSlope]
      push_cast
      ring

/-- **Exact form of the interpolant on a piece.** -/
theorem lipReluNet_on_piece (f : ℝ → ℝ) (N j : ℕ) (hN : 1 ≤ N) (hj : j < N) (x : ℝ)
    (hx : x ∈ Icc ((j : ℝ) / N) (((j : ℝ) + 1) / N)) :
    lipReluNet f N x = f ((j : ℝ) / N) + interpSlope f N j * (x - (j : ℝ) / N) := by
  have hN0 : (0:ℝ) < N := by exact_mod_cast hN
  obtain ⟨hx1, hx2⟩ := hx
  have hsum : ∑ i : Fin N, interpCoeff f N (i : ℕ) * relu (1 * x + -((i : ℕ) : ℝ) / N)
      = ∑ i ∈ Finset.range N, interpCoeff f N i * relu (1 * x + -(i : ℝ) / N) := by
    rw [Fin.sum_univ_eq_sum_range (fun i => interpCoeff f N i * relu (1 * x + -(i : ℝ) / N)) N]
  have hsplit : ∑ i ∈ Finset.range N, interpCoeff f N i * relu (1 * x + -(i : ℝ) / N)
      = ∑ i ∈ Finset.range (j + 1), interpCoeff f N i * relu (1 * x + -(i : ℝ) / N)
        + ∑ i ∈ Finset.Ico (j + 1) N, interpCoeff f N i * relu (1 * x + -(i : ℝ) / N) := by
    rw [Finset.range_eq_Ico, ← Finset.sum_Ico_consecutive _ (Nat.zero_le (j + 1)) hj]
  have hzero : ∑ i ∈ Finset.Ico (j + 1) N, interpCoeff f N i * relu (1 * x + -(i : ℝ) / N) = 0 := by
    refine Finset.sum_eq_zero (fun i hi => ?_)
    have hij : (j : ℝ) + 1 ≤ (i : ℝ) := by
      have : j + 1 ≤ i := (Finset.mem_Ico.1 hi).1
      exact_mod_cast this
    have : 1 * x + -(i : ℝ) / N ≤ 0 := by
      have h1 : x ≤ ((j : ℝ) + 1) / N := hx2
      have h2 : ((j : ℝ) + 1) / N ≤ (i : ℝ) / N := by gcongr
      have : x ≤ (i : ℝ) / N := le_trans h1 h2
      rw [one_mul, neg_div]
      linarith
    rw [relu, max_eq_right this, mul_zero]
  have hlow : ∀ i ∈ Finset.range (j + 1),
      interpCoeff f N i * relu (1 * x + -(i : ℝ) / N)
        = interpCoeff f N i * (x - (i : ℝ) / N) := by
    intro i hi
    have hij : (i : ℝ) ≤ (j : ℝ) := by
      have : i ≤ j := Nat.lt_succ_iff.1 (Finset.mem_range.1 hi)
      exact_mod_cast this
    have : 0 ≤ 1 * x + -(i : ℝ) / N := by
      have h2 : (i : ℝ) / N ≤ (j : ℝ) / N := by gcongr
      rw [one_mul, neg_div]
      linarith
    rw [relu, max_eq_left this]
    ring
  rw [lipReluNet, reluNet, hsum, hsplit, hzero, Finset.sum_congr rfl hlow]
  have hexpand : ∑ i ∈ Finset.range (j + 1), interpCoeff f N i * (x - (i : ℝ) / N)
      = x * (∑ i ∈ Finset.range (j + 1), interpCoeff f N i)
        - (∑ i ∈ Finset.range (j + 1), (i : ℝ) * interpCoeff f N i) / N := by
    rw [Finset.mul_sum, Finset.sum_div, ← Finset.sum_sub_distrib]
    refine Finset.sum_congr rfl (fun i _ => ?_)
    field_simp
  rw [hexpand, sum_interpCoeff, sum_index_interpCoeff, sum_interpSlope]
  field_simp
  ring

/-- **Jackson-type rate for shallow ReLU on Lipschitz targets.** -/
theorem lipschitz_relu_rate (f : ℝ → ℝ) (L : ℝ) (N : ℕ) (hN : 1 ≤ N)
    (hlip : ∀ u ∈ Icc (0:ℝ) 1, ∀ v ∈ Icc (0:ℝ) 1, |f u - f v| ≤ L * |u - v|)
    (x : ℝ) (hx : x ∈ Icc (0:ℝ) 1) :
    |f x - lipReluNet f N x| ≤ 2 * L / N := by
  have hN0 : (0:ℝ) < N := by exact_mod_cast hN
  obtain ⟨hx0, hx1⟩ := hx
  -- choose the piece containing `x`
  obtain ⟨j, hjN, hxj1, hxj2⟩ : ∃ j : ℕ, j < N ∧ (j : ℝ) / N ≤ x ∧ x ≤ ((j : ℝ) + 1) / N := by
    rcases le_or_gt (⌊x * N⌋₊) (N - 1) with hcase | hcase
    · refine ⟨⌊x * N⌋₊, by omega, ?_, ?_⟩
      · rw [div_le_iff₀ hN0]
        exact Nat.floor_le (by positivity)
      · rw [le_div_iff₀ hN0]
        exact le_of_lt (Nat.lt_floor_add_one (x * N))
    · refine ⟨N - 1, by omega, ?_, ?_⟩
      · have hfl : (N : ℝ) ≤ x * N := by
          have : N ≤ ⌊x * N⌋₊ := by omega
          have h2 : ((N : ℕ) : ℝ) ≤ (⌊x * N⌋₊ : ℝ) := by exact_mod_cast this
          exact le_trans h2 (Nat.floor_le (by positivity))
        have hx1' : 1 ≤ x := by nlinarith
        have : ((N - 1 : ℕ) : ℝ) ≤ (N : ℝ) := by
          have : (N - 1 : ℕ) ≤ N := Nat.sub_le _ _
          exact_mod_cast this
        rw [div_le_iff₀ hN0]
        nlinarith
      · have hcast : ((N - 1 : ℕ) : ℝ) + 1 = (N : ℝ) := by
          have hh : (N - 1 : ℕ) + 1 = N := by omega
          have := congrArg (fun m : ℕ => (m : ℝ)) hh
          push_cast at this
          linarith
        rw [hcast, div_self (ne_of_gt hN0)]
        exact hx1
  have hmem : (j : ℝ) / N ∈ Icc (0:ℝ) 1 := by
    constructor
    · positivity
    · rw [div_le_one hN0]
      have : (j : ℝ) ≤ N := by exact_mod_cast le_of_lt hjN
      linarith
  have hmem1 : ((j : ℝ) + 1) / N ∈ Icc (0:ℝ) 1 := by
    constructor
    · positivity
    · rw [div_le_one hN0]
      have : (j : ℝ) + 1 ≤ N := by exact_mod_cast hjN
      linarith
  rw [lipReluNet_on_piece f N j hN hjN x ⟨hxj1, hxj2⟩]
  have hstep : |f x - f ((j : ℝ) / N)| ≤ L / N := by
    have := hlip x ⟨hx0, hx1⟩ ((j : ℝ) / N) hmem
    refine this.trans ?_
    have habs : |x - (j : ℝ) / N| ≤ 1 / N := by
      rw [abs_le]
      constructor
      · have : (0:ℝ) < 1 / N := by positivity
        linarith
      · have h1 : ((j : ℝ) + 1) / N - (j : ℝ) / N = 1 / N := by field_simp; ring
        linarith
    have hL0 : 0 ≤ L := by
      by_contra hneg
      push_neg at hneg
      have h1 := hlip 0 ⟨le_refl 0, by norm_num⟩ 1 ⟨by norm_num, le_refl 1⟩
      have h2 : |f 0 - f 1| ≥ 0 := abs_nonneg _
      simp at h1
      linarith
    calc L * |x - (j : ℝ) / N| ≤ L * (1 / N) := by
          exact mul_le_mul_of_nonneg_left habs hL0
      _ = L / N := by ring
  have hslope : |interpSlope f N j| ≤ L := by
    rw [interpSlope, abs_mul, abs_of_pos hN0]
    have := hlip (((j : ℝ) + 1) / N) hmem1 ((j : ℝ) / N) hmem
    have habs : |((j : ℝ) + 1) / N - (j : ℝ) / N| = 1 / N := by
      rw [show ((j : ℝ) + 1) / N - (j : ℝ) / N = 1 / N by field_simp; ring]
      exact abs_of_pos (by positivity)
    rw [habs] at this
    calc |f (((j : ℝ) + 1) / N) - f ((j : ℝ) / N)| * N ≤ (L * (1 / N)) * N :=
          mul_le_mul_of_nonneg_right this hN0.le
      _ = L := by field_simp
  have hlin : |interpSlope f N j * (x - (j : ℝ) / N)| ≤ L / N := by
    rw [abs_mul]
    have habs : |x - (j : ℝ) / N| ≤ 1 / N := by
      rw [abs_le]
      constructor
      · have : (0:ℝ) < 1 / N := by positivity
        linarith
      · have h1 : ((j : ℝ) + 1) / N - (j : ℝ) / N = 1 / N := by field_simp; ring
        linarith
    have hL0 : 0 ≤ L := le_trans (abs_nonneg _) hslope
    calc |interpSlope f N j| * |x - (j : ℝ) / N| ≤ L * (1 / N) :=
          mul_le_mul hslope habs (abs_nonneg _) hL0
      _ = L / N := by ring
  calc |f x - (f ((j : ℝ) / N) + interpSlope f N j * (x - (j : ℝ) / N))|
      ≤ |f x - f ((j : ℝ) / N)| + |interpSlope f N j * (x - (j : ℝ) / N)| := by
        have := abs_sub (f x - f ((j : ℝ) / N)) (interpSlope f N j * (x - (j : ℝ) / N))
        calc |f x - (f ((j : ℝ) / N) + interpSlope f N j * (x - (j : ℝ) / N))|
            = |(f x - f ((j : ℝ) / N)) - interpSlope f N j * (x - (j : ℝ) / N)| := by
              ring_nf
          _ ≤ |f x - f ((j : ℝ) / N)| + |interpSlope f N j * (x - (j : ℝ) / N)| := this
    _ ≤ 2 * L / N := by
        have : L / N + L / N = 2 * L / N := by ring
        linarith [hstep, hlin]


/-- **Jackson-type rate for depth-2 EML networks on Lipschitz targets.**  For
every `L`-Lipschitz `f` on `[0,1]`, every width `N ≥ 1` and every slack `δ > 0`
there is a depth-2 EML network with `N` chains whose uniform error is at most
`2L/N + δ`.  This is the mission's conjectured Jackson rate in dimension `n = 1`
for the general Lipschitz class; combined with `sqLayer_rate` it shows the
`O(w^{-2})` behaviour is a *smoothness* phenomenon, not a Lipschitz one. -/
theorem eml_depth2_lipschitz_rate (f : ℝ → ℝ) (L : ℝ) (N : ℕ) (hN : 1 ≤ N) (δ : ℝ) (hδ : 0 < δ)
    (hlip : ∀ u ∈ Icc (0:ℝ) 1, ∀ v ∈ Icc (0:ℝ) 1, |f u - f v| ≤ L * |u - v|) :
    ∃ Net : Depth2Net N, ∀ x ∈ Icc (0:ℝ) 1, |f x - Net.eval x| ≤ 2 * L / N + δ := by
  refine emlDepth2_dominates_relu N (fun i => interpCoeff f N (i : ℕ)) (fun _ => 1)
    (fun i => -((i : ℕ) : ℝ) / N) (f 0) 0 f (Icc (0:ℝ) 1) (2 * L / N) δ hδ ?_
  intro x hx
  exact lipschitz_relu_rate f L N hN hlip x hx

## Hypothesis (Hypothesizer)

Depth 2 is exactly the depth at which the EML activation becomes *at least as
expressive as* ReLU: an `exp` unit followed by a `log` unit is a softplus, and
softplus is a uniform `log 2 / M` approximation of a rescaled ReLU.  If so, every
ReLU approximation theorem transfers to depth-2 EML at equal width.

## Experiment (Experimenter)

`log(1 + exp(M t))/M − relu t` at `M = 10`:
  t = −1 → 4.54e-6,  t = 0 → 0.0693 (= log 2 / 10, the maximum),
  t = 1  → 4.54e-6.
The bound `log 2 / M` is attained at `t = 0`, so `scaled_softplus_approx_relu` is
sharp; no smaller constant is possible.

For the interpolation part, `f = x²`, `N = 4`: the ReLU realisation
`lipReluNet` returns `0.0625, 0.25, 0.5625, 1` at the nodes `1/4, 1/2, 3/4, 1`,
i.e. it interpolates exactly, and its maximal error `1/64` is well inside the
proved `2L/N = 1` for `L = 2`.

## Analysis (Analyst)

The transfer costs nothing in width and only an arbitrarily small `δ` in
accuracy, but it costs *weight magnitude*: `M ≈ (Σ|aᵢ|) log 2 / δ`.  This is the
same currency in which the width-2 EML network buys its `O(h²)` accuracy for
`x²` (read-out weight `1/h²`).  Pattern: **EML converts weight magnitude into
approximation power, where ReLU has to spend width.**

## Critique (Critic)

* The emulation bound is uniform on all of `ℝ`, not merely on `[0,1]`, so it is
  not an artefact of the domain.
* `emlDepth2_dominates_relu` quantifies over an arbitrary set `S`, so it does not
  smuggle in compactness.
* The Lipschitz hypothesis is stated pointwise on `[0,1]` rather than through
  `LipschitzOnWith`, which keeps the statement elementary and avoids any
  hypothesis about behaviour of `f` outside `[0,1]`.
* Weakness acknowledged: `2L/N` is a factor 2 off the optimal `L/(2N)` for the
  interpolant; sharpening needs a two-sided estimate at the node nearest to `x`,
  not the left node.
-/
